name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,834

clue.text: Relief, partner's rewound programme of course

indicators.note: A tape rewound runs back the way it came, so the letters in front of the word are read from their far end.

blocks.note: a sub is the relief brought on for somebody else
an ally is a partner, and the possessive s goes along with it

explanation.surface: A partner has wound the recorded programme back, to everybody's relief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' reads as the throwaway 'naturally' and is carrying a course of study. The apostrophe-s of 'partner's' is not punctuation here — its S is the last letter of the answer before the turn.
explanation.definitionFit: A syllabus is the printed programme of a course, the list of what will be covered week by week.

clue.text: Lord piled up roughly cut grass for cattle

indicators.note: A pile is built from the bottom, and in a down entry that means these letters are read upwards, back to front.

blocks.note: to hew is to cut roughly, with an axe rather than a blade
hay is cut grass dried for winter feed

explanation.surface: A lord's grass, roughly cut and stacked up as feed for his cattle.
explanation.walkthrough: Yahweh is the Hebrew name of God, written in scripture as the four consonants YHWH. English bibles print LORD in small capitals wherever that name stands, which is what lets one word define the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Yahweh is the God of the Hebrew Bible, the name English versions render as 'the LORD'.

clue.text: Without zip, teach girl knots

indicators.note: To knot something is to tangle it up, and tangled letters do not come out in the order they went in.

blocks.note: nine letters of raw material, the full count

explanation.surface: An instructor with no energy teaching a girl how to tie knots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knots' looks like the subject of the lesson and is the instruction instead. Zip is the energy sense, nothing to do with fasteners; lethargy comes from the Greek for drowsy forgetfulness.
explanation.definitionFit: Zip is get-up-and-go, and a lethargic person has none of it — slow, heavy and hard to rouse.

clue.text: Piper, say, keeps playing tune one loaded

indicators.note: What a thing keeps it holds inside itself, so the pieces that follow go within the word before it.

blocks.note: Billie Piper, the British singer turned actress, is a Piper by way of example
a show playing at the theatre is on
an air is a tune, the old word for a melody

explanation.surface: A piper keeps playing the same tune to a listener who is thoroughly loaded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loaded' is drunk in the surface and rich in the answer, and 'Piper' is a surname rather than a musician. Billie Piper sang before she acted, and was the Doctor's companion when Doctor Who returned.
explanation.definitionFit: Loaded is slang for seriously rich, and a billionaire is one of the people it fits best.

clue.text: Crow finally finds the way from France

indicators.note: Finally points at where a word finishes, so only the letter it ends on is taken.

blocks.note: the letter finds ends on
the how of a job is the way it is done
made from oak, made of oak — the two prepositions stand in for each other
F is the international vehicle code, the letter on the back of a French car

explanation.surface: A crow at last finding its way across from France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crow' is placed to look like the bird making the Channel crossing, and it is the verb — to crow about something. The four pieces arrive in clue order, which is unusual enough to be worth spotting.
explanation.definitionFit: To crow is to trumpet your own success, which is exactly what a show-off does.

clue.text: Money left on account Emily's closing

indicators.note: A name's closing letter is the one it shuts on, and that single letter is all this takes.

blocks.note: in cricket the on side of the field is also called the leg side
a/c is the banking short form of account
the letter Emily ends on

explanation.surface: Money sitting on account as Emily closes up for the day.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface wants 'left' as the opposite of right; it means bequeathed. 'On' for LEG is the cricket field's own synonym and worth filing away, since setters use it in both directions.
explanation.definitionFit: A legacy is money left to somebody in a will, the sum that passes on after a death.

clue.text: Delete third of the longest sentence in story

indicators.note: Delete is a flat order to strike a letter out, and what is struck out does not appear in the answer.

blocks.note: life is the heaviest sentence a British court can pass, the automatic penalty for murder
counting three letters along that sentence lands on F, which is the one to go

explanation.surface: An editor cutting the third of the longest sentences in a story.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word is dressed as a sub-editor at work, and two of them belong elsewhere: the sentence is the courtroom's, the story the nursery's. Three letters, two switches of sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A story in the sense a parent means by 'don't tell stories' is a lie, a made-up account passed off as true.

clue.text: Good thing winners inflict brilliance

blocks.note: G is the short form of good, as on a school report
what winners hand out is a loss to everybody else

explanation.surface: Something good found in the defeats that winners dish out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brilliance' wants to be cleverness and means light bouncing off a surface. Gloss is the shine itself, which is why gloss paint is named for its finish rather than its colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Gloss is the shine a polished surface throws back, brilliance of the literal, light-reflecting kind.

clue.text: The universe's response if the speed of light goes up

indicators.note: In a down entry up is towards the top, so the letter named leaves its place and climbs to the front.

blocks.note: c is the physicist's symbol for the speed of light, the c of E=mc²
a response is a REACTION, here left without the c that has gone up

explanation.surface: A physicist asking how the universe would answer back if light went faster.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a thought experiment and the answer the oldest cosmology there is. One letter does all the work: nothing is added or lost, the c simply moves to the top of the column.
explanation.definitionFit: Creation is everything that was made, taken together — all creation, which is the universe.

clue.text: Wicket taken by bowler? That's unbelievable

definitions.note: The answer is a one-word exclamation and the definition a whole sentence, but both are what somebody blurts out at news they cannot credit.

blocks.note: w is the cricket scorecard's mark for a wicket
a bowler is a stiff round hat

explanation.surface: A wicket falling to the bowler, to general disbelief.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is cricket throughout and only the wicket stays cricket — the bowler is headgear. A bowler hat is the hard domed hat of City clerks, named after the Bowler brothers who blocked it.
explanation.definitionFit: 'What!' is the flat one-word protest people make at something they refuse to believe.

clue.text: Dry balls on toilet seat fabric

indicators.note: In an across clue what is set on something goes after it, so the word following 'on' takes the front and the rest lines up behind.

blocks.note: loo is the everyday British word for the lavatory
sec is the wine label's word for dry, as in demi-sec
an over is the set of six balls bowled from one end in cricket

explanation.surface: Balls left to dry on a lavatory seat.
explanation.walkthrough: A loose cover is the washable slip pulled over an armchair or sofa, so 'seat' is furniture rather than the one in the surface's bathroom. Sec reaches English on wine labels, where it is the opposite of sweet.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose cover is the removable fabric slip that goes over a chair, upholstery you can pull off and wash.

clue.text: Italian's colourful sweet selection - buy one to eat there in Rome

indicators.note: What is eaten is taken inside, so the letters named go within the ones already assembled.

blocks.note: to get a round in is to buy it
the Roman numeral for one
là is Italian for there, the word a Roman would use

explanation.surface: An Italian's tray of brightly coloured ices, to be bought and eaten there in Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: Gelati is the Italian plural of gelato, which is why the definition talks of a selection rather than a single scoop. 'To eat' is the swallowing sense, the clue's own way of saying that something goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Gelati are Italian ice creams, sold by the scoop in pinks and pistachio greens — the sweet display in any Roman gelateria.

clue.text: Facing work, assert it's boring

indicators.note: To bore is to drill a hole through the middle of something, so the letters named end up inside the word before them.

blocks.note: op is short for opus, a composer's work
to pose a claim or a question is to put it forward, to assert it
the word taken down exactly as it stands, then driven into the middle

explanation.surface: Faced with a job of work, somebody insists that the thing is dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' is the drilling sense, not the tedious one the surface wants. 'Facing' is doing prepositional work: the house opposite is the house facing you, which is how an adjective and a preposition can swap.
explanation.definitionFit: The seat opposite is the seat facing you, so the two words do the same job in the same sentence.

clue.text: Most powerful pair on tandem dashed around island

indicators.note: Something dashed has been flung down and broken apart, and letters treated that way land in any order.
Going around a thing means closing over it, so the island's letter is caught up among the ones being flung about.

blocks.note: pr is the shop ticket's short form of pair
eight letters of raw material, nine once the island joins them
I is the map abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: Two riders on a tandem racing round an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pair' is a two-letter abbreviation rather than the couple the surface puts on the bike. The remaining letters include the island's, so the anagram is nine long, not eight.
explanation.definitionFit: Whatever predominates has the upper hand over everything beside it, which is what 'most powerful' describes.

clue.text: Knee-bend in training, lunge once fit

indicators.note: Letters put in training are being worked into a new shape, so they will not stay in the order they were handed over in.

blocks.note: twelve letters of raw material, the full count

explanation.surface: A lunge in the gym from somebody who used to be fit.
explanation.walkthrough: The gym surface does the hiding: a lunge really is a knee-bend, so nothing in the sentence looks out of place. Genuflection comes from the Latin genu, knee — the drop onto one knee made in church.
explanation.definitionFit: To genuflect is to go down briefly on one knee, so a genuflection is that bend of the knee itself.

clue.text: For instance, punching total thug as a benefit

indicators.note: To punch something is to drive straight into it, so the letters doing the punching finish up inside.

blocks.note: to tot up a column of figures is to total it
a hood is a thug, short for hoodlum
e.g. is exempli gratia, Latin for for instance

explanation.surface: A thug taking a punch, and the beating counted as doing him some good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For instance' looks like a speaker clearing his throat and is two letters of the answer. Being to the good is the bookkeeper's phrase — so much in credit once the sums are done.
explanation.definitionFit: Money or advantage reckoned to the good sits on the credit side of the account, counted as a gain.

clue.text: Starry arrogance not just for show?

blocks.note: side is British slang for swagger — 'none of your side'
what is not just for show is the real thing

explanation.surface: Grand airs that may turn out to be genuine rather than put on.
explanation.walkthrough: Sidereal means measured against the stars: a sidereal day is the time the Earth takes to turn relative to them, four minutes shorter than the clock's. The question mark owns the stretch in 'arrogance'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sidereal means of the stars — sidereal time is reckoned by them — so the plain adjective 'starry' covers it.

clue.text: Spooner's trying to sell publican stake in western, perhaps

indicators.note: The Reverend Spooner's trademark slip was to exchange the opening sounds of two words, and that swap is what has to be undone.

blocks.note: to pitch a product is to try to sell it, and the host is the publican behind the bar; trade their opening sounds

explanation.surface: The Reverend Spooner talking a pub landlord into a share of a western film.
explanation.walkthrough: Spooner clues are easiest worked backwards: find the pair of words first, a pitch and a host. William Spooner was an Oxford warden whose tangled announcements made his name a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A hitching post is the upright outside the saloon that a cowboy ties his horse to, a stake you only really meet in westerns.

clue.text: Unbranded cognac Irene guiltily wraps up

indicators.note: To wrap a thing is to fold it out of sight, so the letters wanted are already lying buried in the words themselves.
In a down entry up means read from the bottom, so that buried run is lifted the other way round.

blocks.note: a run of seven letters sits across those three words and is read from the right, cognaC IRENEG

explanation.surface: Irene furtively wrapping up a bottle of cognac.
explanation.walkthrough: Only one word of the hiding place is doing any work beyond concealment, and it is the last: the run needs the g that begins 'guiltily'. A generic medicine is one sold under its chemical name, with no maker's brand on the box.
explanation.definitionFit: A generic product carries no maker's name at all — the plain supermarket packet, unbranded by definition.

clue.text: American 4's marbles

blocks.note: A is the dictionary's short form for American
the answer at 4 down is BILLIONAIRE, and Bill Gates is the American one the clue wants

explanation.surface: An American billionaire's collection of marbles.
explanation.walkthrough: The 4 sends you to 4 down, and it is that answer's meaning you need rather than its letters: one particular billionaire fits. Agates are the banded, swirled marbles children prize most.
explanation.definitionFit: Agates are marbles — the banded stone ones, and the glass copies made to look like them, the prize of any playground set.

clue.text: Write about match in shade of poet's beautiful boat

indicators.note: To write about a subject is to go round it, and letters that go about a word close on either side of it.

blocks.note: to pen a letter is to write it
when two accounts match, they agree

explanation.surface: A reporter writing up a match in the shade of a poet's pretty boat.
explanation.walkthrough: The boat is Edward Lear's: the Owl and the Pussy-cat went to sea in a beautiful pea-green boat. 'Shade' looks like the shadow the writer sits in and is a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Pea-green is the pale green of garden peas, the colour Lear gave the Owl and the Pussy-cat's boat.

clue.text: Bush second, his defeated opponent claims

indicators.note: What a person claims they take to themselves, so the letter beside them is held inside.

blocks.note: Al Gore lost the 2000 American presidential election to George W. Bush
s is the standard short form of second

explanation.surface: The loser of the election insisting that it was Bush who came second.
explanation.walkthrough: The Florida recount is the whole joke, since Gore did win the popular vote, and 'claims' carries both his protest and the instruction. Gorse is the spiny yellow-flowered shrub of British commons and clifftops.
explanation.definitionFit: Gorse is the prickly yellow-flowered shrub that covers British heathland, a bush in the plainest sense.

clue.text: Time global warming stopped, agreed wise man on the radio

indicators.note: What reaches you on the radio is heard and never seen, so the spelling to write down is the one that matches the sound.

blocks.note: aye is the voter's agreed and a sage is a wise man; run the two together and say them

explanation.surface: A broadcast in which some wise man agrees that global warming has stopped.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud the break between the two spoken words falls in a different place from the break in the answer, which is where the disguise lives. 'Aye' is the parliamentary yes — the ayes have it.
explanation.definitionFit: An ice age is a long spell of global cooling, which the setter dates cheerfully as the time warming stopped.

clue.text: Land after air manoeuvres providing cover for marines

indicators.note: Troops on manoeuvres are marched about the field in new formations, and so are these letters.
To provide cover for somebody is to close round them, so the shuffled letters finish up on either side of the piece named.

blocks.note: the eight letters of AFTER AIR in a new order, parting before the last of them
RM is the Royal Marines, Britain's commando force

explanation.surface: An air display followed by a landing, with the marines given cover from above.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Land' is the noun, not the verb the military surface keeps pushing. Terra firma is Latin for solid ground and is what sailors and nervous flyers say when they are back on it.
explanation.definitionFit: Terra firma is dry solid ground as opposed to sea or air, so it names land itself.

clue.text: Young to be given the chair

blocks.note: the newly hatched of a shoal of fish, the ones an angler throws back
the chair is the American electric one, and this is the slang verb for dying in it

explanation.surface: Somebody thought too young to be made chairman.
explanation.walkthrough: The chair reads as the one at the head of the committee table and is the electric one. 'Small fry' is the fish sense still in daily use, which is the easier half to find.
explanation.definitionFit: Fry are newly hatched fish, a shoal's young; and to fry is the American slang for being executed in the electric chair.

clue.text: Bond hot on the heels of every other character in Volante

indicators.note: To follow on somebody's heels is to come immediately behind them, so this letter is set after everything the rest supplies.
It asks for the letters at alternate positions, skipping the ones that fall between them.

blocks.note: vOlAnTe, taking the second letter and every other one after it
H is the letter on the hot tap

explanation.surface: Bond following close behind everybody else in a car called the Volante.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bond' is placed for 007, and a Volante is the convertible Aston Martin, his marque — yet the word means the binding promise. An oath is what a witness swears in the box.
explanation.definitionFit: An oath is a sworn promise, and a person's bond is the same thing: my word is my bond.

clue.text: 3 barks from the back yard

indicators.note: Reading from the back means starting at the far end, so that word runs the other way.

blocks.note: to bark a tree is to strip it, as peeling strips a fruit; both verbs, both third person
y is the short form of yard

explanation.surface: A dog barking out at the back of the yard.
explanation.walkthrough: The 3 points at 3 down, whose answer LETHARGIC is the definition here. The barks are a tree's rather than a dog's, which is the swap the back yard is there to hide.
explanation.definitionFit: 3 down is LETHARGIC, and a sleepy person is exactly that: heavy-eyed, slow and with no energy to spare.

clue.text: A hundred American lawyers in Utah look sharp

indicators.note: In puts what comes before it inside the word that follows, which has to open up to take it.

blocks.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
the state's name taken whole, then opened up
a DA is a district attorney, the prosecutor in an American county court, and here there is more than one

explanation.surface: A hundred American lawyers in Utah, smartening themselves up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look sharp' is the dapper sense, not the drill sergeant's order to hurry. Dash in this phrase is the Victorian one meaning showy display, the impression a fine coat makes on a street.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut a dash is to make a striking impression by how you are turned out, which is to look sharp.
